passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it grants legal relief in circumstances that classical contract theory would regard as unenforceable. Under classical doctrine, a promise is enforceable only when it is supported by consideration — that is, when the promisee has given something of value in exchange for the promisor's commitment. Promissory estoppel departs from this requirement by protecting a promisee who has reasonably relied upon a promise to their detriment, even if no formal exchange of value occurred. Courts in the United States first articulated this principle in the early twentieth century, and it was later codified in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, which provides that a promise is binding if the promisor should reasonably have expected it to induce reliance, and if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement of the promise.

The doctrine's expansion has not proceeded without difficulty. Courts applying promissory estoppel must resolve at least two recurring tensions. First, they must determine how substantial the promisee's reliance must be before estoppel is warranted. Some jurisdictions require that the promisee demonstrate a significant and irreversible change in position — quitting stable employment, for instance, or relocating a household — while others are prepared to extend relief for more modest acts of reliance. This divergence reflects a genuine disagreement about whether the doctrine should primarily restore the promisee to the position they occupied before the promise was made, or whether it should, on occasion, enforce the expectation interest fully, placing the promisee in the position they would have occupied had the promise been kept. The former measure yields reliance damages; the latter yields expectation damages. Courts have not resolved this question uniformly.

A second tension concerns the role of promissory estoppel in commercial settings. In a 2001 case in Illinois, a supplier argued that it had acted in reasonable reliance on a buyer's assurance that a long-term contract would be formalized, and sought expectation damages when the buyer withdrew. The court declined to award full expectation damages, reasoning that sophisticated commercial parties are presumed to appreciate that preliminary assurances do not bind, and that extending estoppel broadly in such contexts would undermine the careful risk allocations that commercial contracts are designed to achieve. This ruling, while defensible on its own terms, risks leaving meritorious claims without remedy when the promisee genuinely lacked the bargaining power to insist on a formal agreement. One hopes that future courts will calibrate the doctrine more sensitively to the relative sophistication of the parties involved, rather than applying a categorical exclusion that treats all commercial actors as equally capable of self-protection.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was first articulated in early twentieth-century American courts and later codified in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel, while a legitimate departure from classical contract theory, has generated unresolved tensions in its application that courts have addressed inconsistently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts should abandon the consideration requirement entirely and rely on promissory estoppel to enforce all promises that induce reasonable reliance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commercial parties should not be permitted to invoke promissory estoppel because they are presumed to understand that preliminary assurances are not binding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The primary distinction between reliance damages and expectation damages is the central problem that courts face when applying promissory estoppel.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces promissory estoppel as a doctrinal departure from classical contract theory, then traces two recurring tensions in its application — the measure of damages and its use in commercial settings — and closes with the author's assessment that courts have handled these tensions inconsistently. B integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: Too narrow — this captures only the historical background in paragraph one, not the passage's evaluative argument.
explanations.C: Too strong and unsupported — the author never advocates abandoning the consideration requirement altogether.
explanations.D: Restates the Illinois court's holding as if it were the author's thesis; the author actually criticizes this categorical approach.
explanations.E: Too narrow — the damages distinction is one of two tensions discussed and is not identified as the central problem.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the Restatement (Second) of Contracts provides that a promise is binding when which one of the following conditions is met?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisee has given consideration of equal or greater value than the promise itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisee has quit stable employment or relocated a household in reliance on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promisor could reasonably have anticipated that the promise would induce reliance, and injustice can be avoided only by enforcement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both parties are of unequal sophistication and the weaker party lacks bargaining power.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promise was made in a commercial setting and was subsequently memorialized in writing.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that the Restatement provides that a promise is binding if the promisor should reasonably have expected it to induce reliance, and if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement. C is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: This restates the classical consideration requirement, which promissory estoppel explicitly displaces.
explanations.B: These are examples of substantial reliance discussed in paragraph two as a jurisdictional standard, not the Restatement's definition.
explanations.D: The relative sophistication of parties is discussed as a factor the author recommends, not as a Restatement condition.
explanations.E: No such requirement appears in the passage; this introduces details not stated anywhere in the text.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A promisee who relocates a household in reliance on a promise should always receive full expectation damages rather than mere reliance damages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A commercial party that lacked meaningful bargaining power may have a meritorious promissory estoppel claim even if it is a business entity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts should eliminate promissory estoppel in commercial settings and restrict the doctrine to purely personal transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The consideration requirement of classical contract law is on the whole a just and adequate mechanism for distributing contractual risk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preliminary assurances in commerce should be treated as fully binding promises whenever they are made in written form.

explanations.correct: The author criticizes the Illinois court's categorical exclusion for leaving meritorious claims without remedy when the promisee genuinely lacked bargaining power, and calls for calibration based on relative sophistication. This implies that a commercial party lacking bargaining power may still deserve relief — regardless of its status as a business entity.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author does not claim relocation always warrants expectation damages; the passage merely lists relocation as an example of substantial reliance in some jurisdictions.
explanations.C: The opposite of the author's position — the author wants more sensitive calibration, not categorical exclusion.
explanations.D: The passage treats the consideration requirement as a baseline that promissory estoppel appropriately departs from in some cases; it does not endorse the requirement as fully adequate.
explanations.E: Nothing in the passage suggests that written form transforms a preliminary assurance into a binding promise.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the Illinois court's 2001 ruling can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unqualified disapproval, because the ruling disregarded well-established precedent on promissory estoppel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cautious approval tempered by concern that the ruling may be extended beyond the circumstances that justified it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualified acceptance of the ruling's underlying reasoning combined with concern that its categorical application may produce unjust outcomes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strong endorsement, because the ruling correctly recognizes that commercial parties should never be permitted to invoke promissory estoppel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Indifference, because the ruling applies only to a narrow category of commercial transactions that are unlikely to recur.

explanations.correct: The author writes that the ruling is 'defensible on its own terms' — an acknowledgment of its rationale — but then criticizes the risk of leaving meritorious claims without remedy, calling for calibration rather than categorical exclusion. C captures this dual stance precisely.
explanations.A: Too strong in both valence and rationale — the author does not call it a violation of precedent, and offers partial acceptance.
explanations.B: Partially accurate in tone but misdescribes the concern: the author worries about categorical application to all commercial parties, not extension beyond original circumstances.
explanations.D: This echoes the court's apparent position, not the author's, who explicitly criticizes a categorical commercial exclusion.
explanations.E: The author's closing call for future courts to calibrate the doctrine shows engagement, not indifference.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origin is traced; two applications of the doctrine are compared; the author concludes that the doctrine should be abolished.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined and distinguished from classical contract theory; two tensions arising in its application are identified and illustrated; the author offers a prescriptive assessment of one tension.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legal controversy is introduced; competing judicial opinions are presented in full; the author synthesizes the opinions and proposes a new rule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a single case study is analyzed in depth; the author generalizes from that case to propose a universal standard.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The inadequacies of classical contract law are catalogued; promissory estoppel is proposed as a complete remedy; objections to the doctrine are raised and then dismissed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph one defines promissory estoppel and contrasts it with the classical consideration requirement. Paragraph two identifies the first tension (measure of reliance and damages) and illustrates it with examples from divergent jurisdictions. Paragraph three identifies the second tension (commercial context), illustrates it with the 2001 Illinois case, and closes with the author's evaluative prescription about calibrating the doctrine. B accurately captures this three-part structure.
explanations.A: The author does not call for abolition of the doctrine — this misidentifies the concluding move.
explanations.C: The passage does not present competing judicial opinions 'in full'; nor does it propose a new formal rule.
explanations.D: The Illinois case is one illustration among others, not an extended case study from which a universal standard is derived.
explanations.E: The passage does not catalogue inadequacies of classical contract law broadly, and promissory estoppel is not presented as a complete remedy.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 2001 Illinois case serves primarily to illustrate which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The general principle that commercial parties are always better positioned than non-commercial parties to protect their legal interests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tension between the doctrine's potential to protect parties who lack bargaining power and courts' reluctance to extend it in commercial settings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The historical development of promissory estoppel from its early twentieth-century origins to its modern commercial applications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proposition that expectation damages are always preferable to reliance damages in cases involving preliminary assurances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The conflict between state and federal courts over the proper scope of promissory estoppel in commercial transactions.

explanations.correct: The Illinois case is introduced to illustrate the second tension identified in paragraph three: courts' reluctance to apply promissory estoppel broadly in commercial settings, which risks leaving meritorious claimants — particularly those lacking bargaining power — without remedy. B captures both sides of the tension.
explanations.A: This overstates what the case illustrates; the author specifically questions whether all commercial parties are equally capable of self-protection.
explanations.C: The historical development is traced in paragraph one; the Illinois case functions to illustrate the commercial-setting tension, not history.
explanations.D: The case does not establish a preference for expectation over reliance damages; the court in fact declined to award expectation damages.
explanations.E: No state-federal conflict is discussed in the passage; both paragraphs address court practices without invoking federalism.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the Illinois court's reasoning as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases have been awarded by courts in other jurisdictions without any measurable disruption to commercial contracting practices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The supplier in the Illinois case had retained legal counsel throughout the negotiations and was aware that no formal contract had been signed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Classical contract theory was developed primarily to protect individual consumers rather than sophisticated commercial entities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many commercial disputes involving preliminary assurances are resolved through arbitration rather than litigation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some jurisdictions require parties to commercial contracts to include written disclaimers stating that preliminary negotiations are not binding.

explanations.correct: The Illinois court's reasoning rests on the premise that broadly extending promissory estoppel in commercial settings would undermine the careful risk allocations that commercial contracts achieve. If expectation damages have been awarded in other commercial jurisdictions without disrupting contracting practices, this directly undercuts the court's central concern about destabilizing commercial arrangements.
explanations.B: This strengthens the court's reasoning by suggesting the supplier was sophisticated enough to understand the risk — it supports, not undermines, the court's position.
explanations.C: The historical purpose of classical contract theory is irrelevant to whether promissory estoppel disrupts commercial risk allocations.
explanations.D: The prevalence of arbitration does not speak to whether courts should award expectation damages when disputes do reach litigation.
explanations.E: The existence of disclaimer requirements in some jurisdictions is consistent with the court's view that commercial parties should protect themselves through formal mechanisms; this neither undermines nor clearly supports the court's reasoning.
